Permutation Test for Network Comparison

Source: R/permutation_test.R
permutation.Rd

permutation() tests whether two networks differ more than chance would produce. The sequences (or, for association networks, the rows) behind both networks are pooled, the group labels are shuffled iter times, both networks are re-estimated on every shuffle, and each observed difference is compared with the shuffled ones. It tests every edge, the network as a whole and, with measures, the nodes' centralities.

It compares two netobjects from build_network() estimated with the same method on the same nodes, for every built-in method and for registered estimators whose result keeps the data (cleaned_data, see register_estimator()). A netobject_group (or an mcml, converted with as_tna()) is tested pair by pair: every pair of its groups when y is NULL, or the groups of the same name in a second netobject_group. Two wtna_mixed results of wtna() are tested on their transition and co-occurrence networks, and two net_edge_betweenness() results on their edge betweenness.

A small p-value says that the observed difference is larger than the shuffles produce; it does not say how large or how probable the difference is, which bayes_compare() estimates. With many edges, some fall below alpha by chance: set adjust to correct for that. The shuffle treats every sequence as exchangeable; when sequences are nested in persons or teams, set actor, and see what the nesting changes with permutation_diagnostics().

Usage

permutation(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  iter = 1000L,
  alpha = 0.05,
  paired = FALSE,
  adjust = "none",
  measures = NULL,
  nlambda = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  actor = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_permutation'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_permutation'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_permutation_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_permutation_group'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'wtna_perm_mixed'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'wtna_perm_mixed'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

x

The first network: a netobject from build_network() (a bare cograph_network is converted to one), a netobject_group or mcml, a wtna_mixed, or a net_edge_betweenness() result. For the print() methods: a net_permutation, net_permutation_group or wtna_perm_mixed.

y

The second network, of the same kind as x, estimated with the same method on the same nodes (their order may differ); other methods or nodes raise an error. Default NULL: when x is a netobject_group or an mcml, every pair of its groups is tested. When both are netobject_groups, the groups present in both under the same name are tested, and having none in common raises an error.

iter

The number of shuffles, at least 2. Default 1000. The smallest attainable p-value is 1 / (iter + 1).

alpha

The significance level, strictly between 0 and 1, that marks an edge or centrality as significant (sig, diff_sig) and that the nestimate_few_actors warning is checked against. It does not change the p-values. Default 0.05.

paired

Whether the two networks hold paired observations (the i-th sequence or row of x with the i-th of y, such as the same people measured twice). Each shuffle then swaps the two members of a pair at random instead of shuffling all labels, so x and y need the same number of sequences (after concat) or rows; otherwise an error is raised. It cannot be combined with actor, of which it is the special case of one actor per pair. Default FALSE.

adjust

The multiplicity correction for the p-values, a method of stats::p.adjust(): "none" (default), "holm", "hochberg", "hommel", "bonferroni", "BH", "BY" or "fdr". The correction runs over the tested edges: the cells non-zero in either network (a self-loop included), each pair counted once in an undirected network, whose matrix stays symmetric. Cells zero in both networks keep their raw p-value, 1. The centrality p-values are corrected separately, over all states and measures. Any other value raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input before anything runs.

measures

Centrality measures to test as well as the edges: any of "OutStrength", "InStrength", "ClosenessIn", "ClosenessOut", "Closeness", "Betweenness", "BetweennessRSP", "Diffusion" and "Clustering" ("InCloseness" and "OutCloseness" are accepted for "ClosenessIn" and "ClosenessOut"), or "all" for the nine. Default NULL (edges only). Every state and measure gets the observed difference, an effect size and a p-value from the same shuffled networks as the edge test. The centralities are computed as by net_centrality() with its defaults: self-loops left out, heavier edges as shorter steps, and Diffusion range-normalised to 0–1 in each network. An unknown name raises an error, and so does any measures with net_edge_betweenness() input.

nlambda

Ignored, kept so existing calls run. Default NULL. The shuffled glasso networks use the nlambda the networks were built with (see Details); a value other than NULL gives a warning of class nestimate_ignored_argument.

seed

An integer that makes the shuffles reproducible. Default NULL. The session's own random stream is left as it was; with grouped input each pair, or each shared group, is tested from the same seed.

actor

The column identifying the actor each sequence belongs to: the person whose sessions they are, or the team of a student. It is looked up in the network's metadata (such as "student_id" when sessions are nested in students, or "Group" for students nested in teams) and then in its wide sequence data. Whole actors are then shuffled, and the ICC and design effect are reported; see the sections Nested data and actor and ICC and design effect. Default NULL: sequences are shuffled one by one. A value that is not one column name, or actor with paired = TRUE, raises an error of class nestimate_bad_actor; a column that is absent or has missing values, nestimate_actor_missing; a column whose values do not give one id per sequence (or, with concat, that joins rows of different actors), nestimate_actor_misaligned; a method other than the transition methods, nestimate_actor_unsupported.

...

For the print() and summary() methods: not used.

object

For the summary() methods: a net_permutation, net_permutation_group or wtna_perm_mixed.

Value

A net_permutation object. print() shows the settings, the number of edges tested and significant, the global test and, with actor, the ICC and design effects; summary() returns the edge table, one row per edge present in either network; cograph::splot() draws the difference network. Grouped input gives a net_permutation_group, a named list of net_permutation results (one per group pair, named "<group i> vs <group j>", when y is NULL; one per shared group name otherwise), whose print() prints each and whose summary() stacks the edge tables with a leading group column naming the pair or group. Two wtna_mixed inputs give a wtna_perm_mixed, the net_permutation results of the transition and cooccurrence networks, whose print() prints both and whose summary() returns a list of their two edge tables. The print() methods return their input invisibly. The net_permutation's fields:

x, y

The two networks compared.

diff

The observed difference matrix, x - y.

diff_sig

The observed difference where p < alpha, else 0.

p_values

The p-value matrix (adjusted when adjust is not "none").

effect_size

The effect-size matrix: the observed difference divided by the SD of the shuffled differences.

summary

The edge table summary() returns: one row per edge present in either network (an undirected network has one row per unordered pair), with columns from, to, weight_x, weight_y, diff, effect_size, p_value and sig.

global

The global test, one row per statistic: statistic ("M", the sum of absolute differences, and "S", the largest absolute difference), observed, and p_value from the same shuffles as the edge test. Absent for edge-betweenness input.

method

The network estimation method ("edge_betweenness" for edge-betweenness input).

source_method

For edge-betweenness input: the source networks' method.

edge_betweenness

For edge-betweenness input: the invert setting and the source method used.

iter, alpha, paired, adjust

The settings used.

actor

The actor column name, or NULL.

n_actors

The number of distinct actors, or NULL.

null_sd

The SD of each edge's shuffled differences (the effect-size denominator), as a matrix.

null_sd_m

The SD of the global statistic M over the shuffles. Absent for edge-betweenness input.

clustering

Only with actor: a one-row data frame with n_sequences, n_actors, design ("between", "within" or "mixed"), icc with icc_ci_lower and icc_ci_upper (how alike the sequences of one actor are), deff_edges (the median design effect over edges), deff_global (the design effect for M) and min_p, the smallest attainable p-value.

clustering_edges

Only with actor: one row per edge of the edge table, with from, to, icc, null_sd_actor, null_sd_sequence and deff.

centralities

Only with measures: a list of stats (one row per state and measure, with state, centrality, diff_true, effect_size and p_value), diffs_true (the observed differences, one row per state and one column per measure) and diffs_sig (the same where p < alpha, else 0).

Details

For transition methods, per-sequence count matrices are computed once and each shuffle only re-sums them, which keeps a large iter fast; the networks' scaling and threshold are applied to every shuffled network as to the observed one. For the other methods the estimator is re-run on every shuffle (cor and pcor through a lighter direct path). For glasso, every shuffled network is estimated as build_network() estimated the observed ones, with x's params (each sample's own lambda path, nlambda, lambda.min.ratio, gamma, penalize.diagonal, refit), so the observed difference and its null come from one estimator (van Borkulo et al. 2022). Two glasso networks built with different settings raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input. A network that rests on one sequence, or one-hot data with no actor or session, has nothing to shuffle and raises an error of class nestimate_single_sequence.

Wide rows combined with params = list(concat = k) are shuffled as the merged sequences the estimator used, keeping their internal joins. A merged sequence must lie within one actor when actor is set (class nestimate_actor_misaligned otherwise), and paired tests need the same number of merged sequences. Both networks must use the same weighted setting (class nestimate_bad_input otherwise).

A refit that fails or produces non-finite weights makes the permutation statistic undefined for that shuffle. The test then raises an error of class nestimate_permutation_failed that reports the number of failed shuffles, and returns no p-values: failed shuffles are neither counted as non-exceedances nor dropped from the null.

For net_edge_betweenness() input, the source networks are shuffled and edge betweenness is recomputed on each shuffle. Both objects must come from the same source method and use the same invert setting.

The centrality block follows the layout of tna::permutation_test(measures = ): a centrality whose shuffled differences do not vary gets an effect size of NaN or Inf, as there, rather than the 0 the edge table uses.

What is tested

Two kinds of question are answered from the same shuffles.

Edge tests

One test per edge: is the difference in this edge's weight, x - y, larger in absolute value than the shuffles produce? summary() reports each with an effect size (the observed difference divided by the SD of the shuffled differences, 0 when that SD is 0) and a p-value, (number of shuffles at least as extreme + 1) / (iter + 1).

Global test

One test for the whole network: do the two networks differ at all? Two statistics: M, the sum of the absolute differences over all cells of the weight matrix (the total amount of difference; an undirected edge counts twice), and S, the largest absolute difference. Being a single test, it needs no multiplicity correction. print() shows it.

The letters follow this function's historical convention. In nct(), M is instead the largest absolute edge difference and S the difference in global strength; the sum of absolute edge differences here measures total edge difference, not a difference in global strength. The smallest attainable p-value is 1 / (iter + 1); with the default iter = 1000 it is 0.000999, meaning that no shuffle came close.

Nested data and actor

Shuffling treats every sequence as an exchangeable unit. When several sequences come from the same actor (sessions of one person, students of one team), actor names the column identifying that actor, and the shuffle respects it (Good, 2005; Anderson & ter Braak, 2003): an actor whose sequences are all in one group moves to the other group as a whole, and an actor with sequences in both groups has their labels shuffled among their own sequences only. Mixed designs combine the two. The observed differences do not change; only the p-values and effect sizes do. With few actors there are few distinct ways to shuffle them, and a warning of class nestimate_few_actors is raised when no p-value could fall below alpha.

actor is available for transition networks built from sequences ("relative", "frequency", "co_occurrence"). On one-hot data the actor column is held per row rather than per unit, so the call raises an error of class nestimate_actor_misaligned. The other methods, association networks ("cor", "pcor", "glasso", ...) among them, do not keep row identifiers after estimation and raise an error of class nestimate_actor_unsupported.

ICC and design effect

With actor, print() also reports:

ICC

The intraclass correlation, the proportion of the total variance that lies between actors (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979). An ICC close to 0 indicates little evidence of a nesting effect. It is the one-way ANOVA ICC of each sequence's transition shares within each group, averaged over edges weighted by edge frequency and jackknife bias-corrected, with a 95% interval from the leave-one-actor-out jackknife (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993).

Design effect

The ratio of the variance of an estimate under the clustered design to its variance had the units been sampled independently (Kish, 1965). Here it is the variance of the shuffled differences when whole actors are moved, divided by the variance when single sequences are moved, both drawn in the same run, reported as the median over edges and for the global statistic M. For equal numbers of sequences per actor m, Kish gives the approximation 1 + (m - 1) * ICC.

Reading the printed output


Permutation Test: Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]
  Iterations: 1000  |  Alpha: 0.05  |  Actor: Group (200 actors)
  Nodes: 9  |  Edges tested: 78  |  Significant: 42
  Global test (networks differ overall?): M = 2.612 (p = 0.000999)  |  ...
  Nesting in Group: ICC = -0.002 [95% CI -0.006, 0.002]  |  between design
  Design effect (1 = nesting does not matter): edges 1.03  |  global 1.20

Line 2: the settings, and the actor column with its number of actors. Line 3: the edges present in either network and how many differ at alpha. Line 4: the global test. Lines 5 and 6, only with actor: the ICC with its interval, whether actors sit in one group (between), in both (within) or either (mixed), and the design effects. With actor, when no p-value can fall below alpha (too few actors, or too small an iter), a last line says so.

References

Anderson, M. J., & ter Braak, C. J. F. (2003). Permutation tests for multi-factorial analysis of variance. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 73(2), 85-113.

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall.

Good, P. (2005). Permutation, Parametric, and Bootstrap Tests of Hypotheses (3rd ed.). Springer.

Kish, L. (1965). Survey Sampling. Wiley.

Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420-428.

van Borkulo, C. D., van Bork, R., Boschloo, L., Kossakowski, J. J., Tio, P., Schoevers, R. A., Borsboom, D., & Waldorp, L. J. (2023). Comparing network structures on three aspects: A permutation test. Psychological Methods, 28(6), 1273-1285.

See also

permutation_diagnostics() to compare the actor-level and ordinary tests side by side; bayes_compare() for the Bayesian complement, which instead of "is this difference more extreme than chance?" answers "how probable is a difference, and how large?"; build_network(), bootstrap_network()

Examples

s1 <- data.frame(V1 = c("A","B","C"), V2 = c("B","C","A"))
s2 <- data.frame(V1 = c("A","C","B"), V2 = c("C","B","A"))
n1 <- build_network(s1, method = "relative")
n2 <- build_network(s2, method = "relative")
perm <- permutation(n1, n2, iter = 10)
# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
d1 <- data.frame(V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE),
                 V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE),
                 V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE))
d2 <- data.frame(V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE),
                 V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE),
                 V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, TRUE))
net1 <- build_network(d1, method = "relative")
net2 <- build_network(d2, method = "relative")
perm <- permutation(net1, net2, iter = 100, seed = 42)
print(perm)
#> Permutation Test: Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]

summary(perm)
